newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine asks foreign aid to reschedule Russia debt.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine asks foreign aid to reschedule Russia debt.

text.p: Ukraine is considering enlisting the help of foreign banks and institutions to restructure its foreign debt to Russia, the first deputy finance minister said on Thursday.

"Right now we are talking with the Russian Federation, as one of our largest creditors, about the possibility of restructuring the debt the Ukrainian government owes it," Mykhailo Honcharuk said at a news conference.
"These talks include the possible participation of international bodies in the restructuring, and the possible participation of various banks," he said.
Ukraine owes Russia $3.5 billion, mostly for energy. About $1.4 billion was rescheduled in 1995 to cover outstanding debt to Russia's Gazprom.
Honcharuk said Ukraine wanted its debt rescheduling to be similar to Russia's debt restructuring by the Paris Club of government creditors and London Club of commercial bank creditors.
Russia has rescheduled around $40 billion over 25 years with the Paris Club and about $35 billion for up to 25 years with the London Club.
"We are investigating the possibility, with other banks, of restructuring Ukraine's debts," Honcharuk said. "There is also interest on the part of banks to work in this direction."

Honcharuk made the comments following a report in the Financial Times newspaper this week that Ukraine was trying to sell up to $350 million of its rescheduled debt to German commercial banks, including Deutsche Bank.
Sources close to the talks said Ukraine had approached German institutions to help reschedule its debt to Russia, but said the matter was at a very early stage.
The sale would take pressure off the country's foreign currency reserves, which would otherwise be used to pay the first part of the $1.4 billion of debt due to Russia this year.
Nearly half of Ukraine's $8.84 billion foreign debt is owed to Russia and Turkmenistan, Ukraine's main suppliers of gas.
Ukraine's parliament this week halted the government from acquiring further foreign credits until it passes a law governing the process in March, but the president can overlook the motion.
